newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: SBC joins other Swiss banks with loss.
newsitem.headline: SBC joins other Swiss banks with loss.

text.p: Swiss Bank Corp. Wednesday joined the other two Swiss banking giants by posting a 1996 loss after taking huge restructuring charges and provisions that should help future growth.

Analysts said SBC was probably best-placed of the big three for recovery. But Swiss banking still faced problems with bad loans due to a flat domestic economy, although a fall in the Swiss franc's value offered hope of an upturn.
SBC, the country's third-largest bank group, posted a group net loss of 1.955 billion Swiss francs ($1.3 billion) compared with a 1.053 billion franc ($714 million) profit in 1995.
Last September SBC forceast that restructuring measures and write-offs totalling 3.3 billion francs ($2.24 billion) would push it into a loss of 1.9 billion ($1.29 billion).

All three big Swiss banks last year pushed ahead with massive writeoffs, job cuts and extra provisioning to try to tackle persistent economic weakness and a chronically depressed domestic real estate sector. All have said that operational improvements were already happening.
SBC's operating profits improved and it is confident of further progress in 1997 toward its medium-term target of an after-tax return on equity of 15 percent.
The group's 1996 after-tax ROE was 10.1 percent.

SBC chief executive Marcel Ospel confirmed an earlier forecast for a 1997 net profit of 1.7 billion francs ($1.2 billion). "I said earlier today that we are on course for our goals. That means that I confirm this profit goal," he told reporters.
Operating profit was up 29 percent to 3.905 billion francs ($2.65 billion) and net after-tax profit before extraordinary items was up 26 percent to 1.328 billion ($900 million).

The biggest contribution to group profits came from SBC Private Banking, which increased net profit by nearly 19 percent to 1.063 billion francs ($721 million). The investment banking division SBC Warburg reported net profit growth of 55 percent to 820 million francs ($556 million).
Last month rival banking giant Union Bank of Switzerland posted a 1996 net loss of 348 million francs ($236 million) after a three billion franc ($2 billion) charge to cover bad domestic loans.
Credit Suisse Group earlier this month reported a 2.59 billion franc ($1.76 billion) loss after extraordinary charges of 5.4 billion ($3.66 billion) for restructuring and bad loan provisions.
Many analysts believe SBC has perhaps adopted the most thorough strategy to tackle Swiss banking's problems.

"I stick to my view that they are most advanced in transforming the company into a new bank with clear, focused entities like private banking and investment banking," said Bank Julius Baer banking analyst Hans Kaufmann.
But he said the banks were still at risk as the economy was showing little sign of a revival and costs were still high, especially at Credit Suisse.
